preamble: Smoothing of the diphthong [ai] to a monophthong [a]/[aː] by loss of the front glide, often with compensatory length. In Old English, Proto-Germanic *ai regularly became ā [ɑː] (*stainaz > stān 'stone'), while Old Frisian and Old Saxon raised it to ē instead. In modern Southern American English, the PRICE vowel /aɪ/ loses its glide to [aː] in many or all environments (ride sounding like 'rod/rad' to other speakers). This glide weakening is Stage 1 of the Southern Vowel Shift.

examples.note: Compare Gothic stáins, Old Norse steinn, Old Frisian stēn.
Compare Old Norse heill, Old Frisian hēl; Modern English whole, hale.
Glide weakening or deletion is the Southern norm; it is favoured before voiced consonants and word-finally and disfavoured before voiceless consonants in many varieties.
